claims.text: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 can be produced by powder metallurgy.
W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr–V-rich precipitates when irradiated near 8 dpa at approximately 300°C.
Precipitate formation in irradiated W38Ta36Cr15V11 is accompanied by irradiation-induced hardening.
Approximately 3 at% Hf should be added to W38Ta36Cr15V11 by replacing part of its V or Cr content.
The Hf-modified alloy can retain an overall nanocrystalline structure after mechanical alloying and sintering.
Hf atoms will preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and dislocations in the W–Ta–Cr–V matrix.
Hf segregation to defect sinks will stabilize grain boundaries and dislocations.
Hf at defect sinks will reduce the local mobility of Cr and V.
Reduced Cr and V mobility will suppress their irradiation-induced clustering into precipitates.
A 3 at% Hf addition will lower or eliminate the density of Cr–V-rich precipitates relative to unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 after irradiation to 8 dpa at approximately 300°C.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain low irradiation-induced hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain radiation resistance comparable to unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The Hf-modified alloy will remain practically manufacturable by powder-metallurgy processing.
The proposed precipitation-suppression effect is applicable up to 8 dpa at temperatures around 300°C.
At doses or temperatures above the proposed limits, increased diffusion may reduce the effectiveness of Hf segregation.
At higher doses or temperatures, the balance between precipitation suppression and manufacturability may change.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis frames the baseline alloy as having low or negligible irradiation hardening that should be preserved, whereas the material_initial_state and baseline describe attendant or significant hardening after irradiation.
